articles.title: IMCWP 24: Contribution of CP Mexico (PCM)
articles.author: MLToday
articles.content: Comrades: We extend our fraternal greetings to all the communist and workers’ parties participating in this International Meeting of Communist and Workers’ Parties. We thank the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Cuba for organizing this 24th IMCWP, despite the very difficult conditions. This initiative arose within the framework of the 150th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto, at the invitation of the Communist Party of Greece. This forum has now been running for over a quarter of a century and has become a fundamental platform for the exchange of opinions and information, under the new conditions in which the international communist movement has had to operate after the predominance of market relations, incompatible with socialist construction, led to the temporary triumph of the counterrevolution in the USSR and other countries. We have come to pay homage to Commander Fidel Castro Ruz on the centenary of his birth. From a very young age, he chose the path of Revolution and internationalism, believing it represented the emancipation and happiness of the Cuban people and workers, and the liberation of Cuba from the ominous chains of imperialism. The popular uprising against the Batista dictatorship—which was sustained by legal and illegal capital, the White House, and the mafia in holy alliance—linked the longed-for independence with socialism, in the era of the historical transition from capitalism to socialism inaugurated by the Great October Socialist Revolution of 1917. This process reaffirmed one of the general laws of revolution: that an intermediate stage between socialism and capitalism is not necessary, as Commander Ernesto Guevara aptly summarized in his maxim, “either socialist revolution or a caricature of revolution.” In fact, in addition to confronting Cuban bourgeois power, US monopolies, and imperialism; The Cuban Revolution and the thought and action of Commander Fidel Castro also brought a questioning of the opportunist line of Browderism and its aftermath, such as class conciliation and reformism within the communist movement in our continent, and also in Cuba. While some petty-bourgeois factions, profiting from the prestige of the Cuban Revolution, sought to deny the indispensable role of the Communist Party in the revolutionary process, and even the revolutionary historical character of the working class, Fidel fought resolutely to bring together the various revolutionary forces into a new Communist Party of Cuba. This party was a continuation of the one founded by Carlos Baliño and Julio Antonio Mella, as the Cuban section of the Third International, and it placed the proletariat at the forefront of the Revolution at all levels, clearly understanding, as the Commander explained on several occasions [1], that there would never again be power of the bourgeoisie, by the bourgeoisie, and for the bourgeoisie, but rather power of the workers, by the workers, and for the workers. Fidel earned the respect of the international communist and revolutionary movement, and his prestige grew even more when, during the temporary defeat of socialist construction in the USSR and Eastern Europe, against all odds, he firmly maintained the socialist leadership of the Cuban revolutionary process, preserving socialist gains and guaranteeing the right to continue socialist construction in the future. This feat was an inspiration to communists in every country. We have much to learn from Fidel, drawing on his thought and action. We also come in this context to reiterate our solidarity with the people of Cuba and with the socialist achievements of the Revolution. The arrival of the US fleet in the Caribbean, and the proclamation by the Trump administration of the New US National Security Doctrine, demonstrate that the fierce competition between capitalist economies led by the US/EU versus so-called multipolar economies, with their conflicts and wars, also involves Latin America. The stated objective of the US in its new doctrine is to expel Chinese capital from the region in order to regain its hegemony. This policy of aggression immediately translated into action, and after the attack on Venezuela—which met with the heroic resistance of 32 Cuban combatants—and the imposition of an ad hoc government , the US turned its attention to Cuba. From then on, week after week, measures were relentlessly adopted to suffocate Cuba, the main weapon being the imposition of a total energy blockade against the Cuban people, which reinforces and intensifies the economic blockade that has now lasted 64 years. Threatening sanctions and tariffs, they have forced several states to yield to pressure, relinquishing their sovereign right to trade freely with third countries. They have attempted to break the revolution by sanctioning leaders and organizations, surgically targeting the entry of productive and financial resources; but they have encountered the wall of a people determined to defend the chosen path. They have even had the cynicism and cowardice to personally attack General Raúl Castro. From its very beginnings in power, the Cuban Revolution faced hostility, economic warfare, and even direct military aggression, but in recent years, this new wave of aggression is the most serious. The response of the people, international solidarity, and communist parties must rise to the occasion, both politically and in concrete terms. For example, the people of Mexico, with the labor movement and communists as their backbone, won sovereignty over this energy resource through the 1938 oil expropriation. Unfortunately, the Mexican state yielded to pressure and suspended oil agreements with Cuba. In response, the grassroots campaign, “ A Ship of Oil for Cuba “, gained prominence, a campaign to which the Mexican Communist Party (PCM) contributed, along with other Mexican organizations, and with the fraternal support of sister parties like the Communist Party of the Workers of the United Workers of Mexico (PCTE). We consider solidarity with Cuba and the defense of its socialist achievements imperative at this time. The initiatives of the Mexican Communist Party (PCM) and the Communist Youth are countless, taking place in workplaces, working-class neighborhoods, and schools, in support of Cuba and against imperialist aggression. Alongside the campaign against Cuba and the war of aggression against the people of Iran, Palestine, and Lebanon, it is also clear that the Trump administration is promoting a campaign against socialism and communism. The ruling classes always keep in mind who their class enemy is. It is true that the ideological mechanisms of imperialism distort history and facts, manipulating them; for example, they present as socialism what is not, such as progressive capitalist initiatives, American social democrats, and even the US Democratic Party itself. However, it is evident that, faced with these distortions and attacks, we communists have the duty to defend our theory, Marxism-Leninism, and our historical objectives: socialism-communism, socialist construction in the USSR, and the characteristics of socialism such as the socialization of the means of production, central and scientific planning of the economy, revolutionary workers’ power, and the dictatorship of the proletariat. Historical experience has shown us the superiority of the new mode of production of socialism-communism for satisfying the needs of the people, for happiness and progress, for unleashing the full potential and creativity of humanity once the system of exploitation is abolished. It has also shown us the suffering of our people when setbacks are tolerated, when counter-revolution gains ground, for socialist construction is not an upward trajectory without a life-or-death struggle against market relations, which are the seed of capitalism, upon which the possibility of temporary regression objectively rests, since accumulation and profit give substance to the petty bourgeoisie, the remnants of the overthrown exploiting classes, mortal enemies of the socialist revolution and of workers’ and people’s power. Let us always keep this bitter lesson in mind. We face difficult times, with an unfavorable correlation, but one that we can modify through action. This should not cloud the historical optimism, based on Marxism-Leninism, regarding the advent of new socialist revolutions. Objective conditions show us imperialist war and acute inter-imperialist competition; the looming signs of capitalist economic crisis; the super-profits of monopolies and the impoverishment of the working class; the devastation of natural resources and the environment; the tragic results of confronting global pandemics under capitalist management; the attacks against working women and migrant workers; the open genocide of a people before the expectant gaze of the world; the galloping development of new productive forces, such as Artificial Intelligence, subordinated to the logic of capital accumulation. But in the face of all these dangers and attacks, a class capable of transforming this situation is moving and resisting, a class that fights and organizes throughout the world. And from all this, only one conclusion can be drawn: Let us strengthen the struggle for socialism-communism, for new socialist revolutions. Cuba will win! Long live Fidel! Long live socialism-communism! [1] For example, in his speech at the Cuba Vive International Youth Festival on August 6, 1995. SOURCE: El Machete – the official press organ of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Mexico (Partido Comunista de México). articles.title: The Stakes Are High in Brazil’s Upcoming Election
articles.author: Alex MacArthur
articles.content: For a time this summer, Brazil’s presidential election seemed Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s to lose, and Latin America’s largest democracy appeared poised to hold its ground while right-wing candidates triumphed in Colombia, Peru, Honduras, Chile, and Panama, and the Left lost its long hold on Bolivia. Before, the race had been steadily tightening between the eighty-year-old president and his forty-five-year-old challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, the blandly affable, lacquered version of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a twenty-seven-year sentence for plotting a coup after his defeat. Even before Flávio’s candidacy was announced, polls had put Lula and Jair neck and neck in a hypothetical runoff, though the elder Bolsonaro was already ankle monitor–bound and barred from candidacy. Brazil With an S But Lula’s campaign was jolted back to life in July 2025, when President Donald Trump, following lobbying by Flávio’s brother, Eduardo, intervened on behalf of the embattled former president. Eduardo — a Texas-based, Steve Bannon–linked convicted criminal — urged American pressure in the name of Brazil’s “political prisoners,” and soon Trump announced 50 percent tariffs on Brazilian imports, followed by financial sanctions on Alexandre de Moraes, the supreme court justice overseeing Bolsonaro’s trial. Lula’s government seized on the affront and made quick work of Trump’s political gift. Within a day of the tariff announcement, it had released an advertisement chiding the gringos for spelling Brasil with a Z; here, the narrator explained, it was spelled with an “S” — for sovereignty. Social media was plastered with images of colossal American flags unfurled at Bolsonaro rallies. And, in a televised address to the nation, Lula declared, “Brazil has only one owner — the Brazilian people.” His message was forceful and unabashedly nationalist, while the Bolsonaro family’s appeals to Washington made its own professions of national pride look pathetically conditional. The strategy seemed to have worked, at least temporarily. By August 2025, a Quaest poll put Lula 12 points ahead of Bolsonaro in a hypothetical runoff. Then, the following May, Flávio’s death knell seemed to sound when The Intercept revealed that he had solicited $24 million from Daniel Vorcaro, the disgraced Banco Master owner jailed on suspicion of multibillion-dollar fraud. In a turn almost too obliging to be true, it was revealed that the massive sum was solicited to fund Dark Horse , a lavish, soapy propaganda film about Flávio’s father’s rise and survival of an assassination attempt starring Jim Caviezel, who played Jesus in Mel Gibson’s The Passion of the Christ . Flávio had publicly denied having personal contact with the banker. Yet the day before Vorcaro was arrested while preparing to board a private jet bound for Malta, Flávio had sent the banker a WhatsApp message reading, “Brother, I am and always will be with you.” In a country particularly sensitive to political corruption scandals, and with voters uninspired by either candidate, the morass seemed close to the worst thing that could have happened to Flávio. In Datafolha’s next survey, Lula broke once more from tied runoff projections, gaining a 4-point advantage. But the political blaze soon spread toward Lula. On September 1, newly disclosed messages recovered by federal police showed Vorcaro seeking advice and intervention from Justice Alexandre de Moraes, even asking whether he should leave the country. Moraes’s replies were not recovered, and he denied acting on the banker’s behalf, but file metadata also indicated that a draft of his wife’s firm’s whopping R$131 million contract with Banco Master had been edited under a user profile bearing the justice’s name. Though the Banco Master scandal implicates Flávio and not Lula, it has become particularly damaging for the latter because Lula is seen as a key ally of Moraes. The jurist has attracted controversy for his role in overseeing Bolsonaro’s prosecution and helping annul the ginned-up charges that led to Lula’s imprisonment until 2019. The most recent polls once again show Lula and Flávio at a stalemate, leaving observers of Brazilian politics waiting either for another sordid revelation, or the very likely possibility of another bumbling intervention from Washington. Lula’s campaign has already had to contend with a right-dominated media at home and interference from abroad. Most recently, Meta inexplicably blocked his campaign social media account for a period less than two weeks before the election, then lifted the ban. This past week, intelligence officials in Brasilia have briefed French and German officials on possible American and Russian attempts to influence the elections. But the preoccupation with scandal that has defined coverage of the election also obscures a more stubborn problem for the incumbent. He has a substantial record to defend, and yet considerable difficulty persuading Brazilians that his leadership made their lives better. Brazil’s economy has fared anomalously well by regional standards. Unemployment stood at just 5.3 percent in the quarter through August, and between 2023 and 2024, 8.6 million people were lifted out of poverty. Lula restored increases in the minimum wage above inflation, expanded payments to families with young children, and secured a significant tax exemption for low-income people. He has continued the tangible improvements that made him the most popular president in Brazilian history during his second term. Yet slowing inflation has not undone years of rising prices, while expensive credit eats into what savings families have. By June, debt repayments excluding mortgages absorbed more than a quarter of aggregate household income. Meanwhile, the war with Iran has put renewed pressure on prices. Lula has not been able to satisfy his constituents in part because he is caught representing the interests of two distinct groups. To the cautious financiers and industry leaders that help decide Brazil’s elections, he must be a solidly establishment figure — the levelheaded custodian of an economy whose debts must be paid. To the workers that fueled his political rise and are fed up with the stasis and complacency of a power-mongering, wealth-hoarding few, he must offer clear material support and evidence that things will change. And though the Economist , following much of the anglophone press, has described him as a “doddering leftie” trying to best a “vengeful nepo-baby,” much of the Brazilian left has found Lula altogether too accommodating to the institutions that have failed them As early as 2010, early leaders on the left wing of Lula’s Workers Party (PT) began lamenting that, in the words of Plínio de Arruda Sampaio, “The leadership abandoned the PT’s project and embraced the pursuit of power.” The metalworker who lost a finger on the job and forged his political reputation rousing crowds of union workers in the late 1970s is now having difficulty convincing voters that he hasn’t grown too comfortable with the establishment he once promised to challenge. Nonetheless, Flávio’s stubborn buoyancy in the race should be cause for alarm well beyond the Left. For all his air of managerial sobriety, the dutiful heir could prove far more destructive to Brazilian democracy than his father. During his presidency, Jair Bolsonaro threatened to disobey judicial rulings, defamed the country’s voting system, and promoted military officials who were later convicted alongside him for a coup conspiracy that included plans to assassinate Lula. But when he entered office in 2019, his authoritarian ambitions were constrained by solid institutions built to withstand attempts to erode democracy. Principally, he was checked by an unusually powerful supreme court, armed with sweeping constitutional and criminal jurisdiction under the 1988 Constitution that was adopted after decades of military dictatorship. But much has changed since 2019, and those restraints can no longer be taken for granted. Nor can the survival of the democracy they helped preserve. To begin with, regardless of the presidential outcome, the Chamber of Deputies is expected to remain dominated by the center and Right, while the Right could substantially strengthen its position in the Senate. There, Flávio has explicitly campaigned to build a Bolsonarista coalition willing to impeach Moraes and other supreme court justices. Even without an impeachment majority, a victorious Flávio could gut the court. Two of its eleven justices were appointed by his father, three reach compulsory retirement age by the end of 2030, and one seat remains vacant. If that vacancy survives Lula’s term, Flávio could appoint four justices — with Senate approval — bringing the number chosen by the family to six, a majority. For a court that has ordered a sitting congressman’s arrest, blocked social media accounts, and suspended X throughout the country, and that has the power to do much else, such capture would give Flávio the power to govern with impunity. With control of the courts and congress, “democratic backsliding” is about the best outcome one could hope for. Freedom of speech and of dissent would be eroded. Jair routinely smeared and discredited journalists, even weaponizing dictatorship-era censorship laws. Alongside the building of five El Salvador–style megaprisons, Flávio has proposed barring parts of school curricula that conflict with parents’ religious or moral beliefs. He has also sought to replace racial quotas in public-service recruitment with income-based preferences and, in a 2011 interview, called the sight of two men kissing “disgusting.” Abroad, Flávio’s flimsy nationalism would likely give way to vassalage to Washington. In June, he wrote to Marco Rubio offering to place his prospective transition team “immediately at your disposal” to negotiate a trade and investment agreement. But following Washington into confrontation with Beijing could prove expensive for Brazil. China has eclipsed the United States as a more reliable market for Brazilian exports, buying nearly 29 percent in 2025 against America’s 11 percent, and Chinese companies invested another $6.1 billion into Brazilian infrastructure that year. The most lasting and globally reaching damage, however, would be environmental. Flávio has dismissed human-caused global warming and mocked the idea that forests generate rainfall, even though reduced rainfall is already harming Brazilian soybean yields. He has coauthored a bill to open mandatory vegetation reserves on rural properties to clearing and backed proposals restricting indigenous claims to ancestral land, alongside expanding oil and gas infrastructure and legalizing fracking. If his father’s presidency offers anything like a preview, the consequences will be disastrous. Jair hobbled environmental enforcement, making illegal clearing easier and punishment less likely. As a result, annual deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon surged by 54 percent between 2018 and 2022, reaching a fifteen-year high in 2021. Further destruction could help push the forest beyond recovery. A study published in Nature this May found that warming of 1.5–1.9°C above preindustrial levels, combined with the clearing of roughly a quarter of the Amazon — which stores carbon equivalent to roughly fifteen to twenty years of global emissions — could trigger widespread ecological collapse. No subsequent government can simply replace vanished rainforest or recapture lost carbon. Yet a Bolsonaro restoration is by no means assured. The coalition that returned Lula to office — organized labor, the rural and urban poor, and progressive sections of the middle class — has frayed but retains considerable strength. Its roots run especially deep in the northeast, where Lula’s Bolsa Família program has long supplemented the meager incomes of working families. It remains to be seen, however, whether right-leaning women will see through Flávio’s shallow attempts to win their votes by mentioning his mother, in an attempt to erase the caustically sexist — and eminently unpopular — legacy of his father from their minds. Nor is it clear that the next Vorcaro WhatsApp screenshot will matter more to voters than the price of groceries or the prospect of getting home safely. At the height of the dictatorship, as military police tortured and jailed dissidents, Chico Buarque released “Apesar de Você,” a somber but resolute samba. To slide the track past state censors, it clothed a resonant challenge to the regime in a quarrel between lovers. “Despite you,” he sang, “tomorrow will be another day.” The censors eventually caught on and banned it. But by then, a hundred thousand copies had sold. articles.title: West Point’s Honor Code Taught the Military to Lie
articles.author: Jasper Craven
articles.content: On May 12, 1962, General Douglas MacArthur strode into the West Point mess hall and delivered a stirring farewell address before an audience of more than two thousand cadets. It had been just over a year since another famed former general, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, had famously delivered his own closing warning about industry’s capture of the Pentagon. Now MacArthur seemed worried about the corruption of the American soldier’s soul — the death of honor itself. Honor was everything to MacArthur. Between 1919 and 1922, as West Point superintendent, he built cadet life around the academy’s hallowed motto, “Duty, Honor, Country.” He further instituted a cadet honor code and attendant honor boards, a quasi-judicial trial system meant to discourage unethical behavior and promote a culture of leadership among fledgling recruits. While honor is traditionally equated with honesty, integrity, and accountability, it doesn’t require any of these things by definition. Rather, it denotes fidelity to an institution’s core rites and standards, making it a fragile, fungible concept whose strictures shift depending on who is giving the orders. In the mess hall that day, MacArthur conjured honor in its purest form, urging the sea of cadets before him “to learn to stand up in the storm, but to have compassion on those who fall; to master yourself before you seek to master others; to have a heart that is clean, a goal that is high.” He called upon them “to be modest so that you will remember the simplicity of true greatness, the open mind of true wisdom, the meekness of true strength.” MacArthur was a fearsome figure, but like any good military mind, he knew the importance of building soldiers with camaraderie, humility, and intelligence. In his stint as West Point superintendent, MacArthur cut down on hazing and expanded academic freedom. He took the education of these warriors in training seriously, even fortifying the humanities as a critical part of their moral development. For the first time, he provided cadets with access to the daily newspapers, a policy that was viciously opposed by a cadre of influential graduates who prized West Point’s insularity. After just three years on the job, that influential cadre, now ensconced in the War Department, transferred MacArthur to the Philippines and reversed his dictate. MacArthur’s ideal of the honorable, well-read, and well-rounded officer was an inspiring conception of service but one that would soon come under grave threat from West Point’s superintendent, William Westmoreland, who, a year after MacArthur’s speech, departed the school to run a campaign in Vietnam racked by war crimes, cooked books, and countless strategic failures. During a sojourn to MacArthur’s apartment at the Waldorf Astoria just before this appointment, the wizened general told Westmoreland that the war in southeast Asia was “fraught with hazards” and could only be won with a “scorched earth policy.” Despite Westmoreland’s profound shortcomings and corruption, he, like many other military architects in Vietnam, would retire in good standing, his reputation helpfully revised via a fawning biography written by West Point’s chair of American history. As the war corroded both honesty and integrity throughout the ranks, heady notions like honor were reduced to meaningless platitudes. President Richard Nixon frequently invoked the vagaries of honor to mask Vietnam’s discredited premise and the degenerate killing that proliferated. When, on January 23, 1973, Nixon announced the end of the war in a short but defiant speech, he used the phrase “peace with honor” five times. The same year as Nixon’s speech, Captain Michael Rose, a young Air Force Academy graduate studying at New York University Law School, published A Prayer for Relief , a damning 253-page investigation into the dysfunctions of MacArthur’s beloved Cadet Honor Code. Over months, Rose collected interviews and intelligence from major training grounds for future military brass, among them all five service academies, including West Point and the Air Force Academy, plus the Virginia Military Institute and the Citadel. His inquiry was powerfully cosigned by a contingent of federal lawmakers, who explicitly counseled military schools to accommodate Rose’s requests for access. They did so begrudgingly, especially at West Point, which actively frustrated his efforts. “The military police there were following me,” he said. West Point also refused to connect Rose to James Pelosi, a cadet then facing a gauntlet of hazing for failing to immediately put down his pencil at the conclusion of a test. Rose ultimately managed to sneak into West Point’s Camp Buckner, a training facility a few miles from the academy on Lake Popolopen, where he went tent to tent one night looking for Pelosi until he found him. “Then he and I went into the latrine, and I tape-recorded him for an hour.” Pelosi’s assessment of military honor was unsparing. “I’m disillusioned with the air of elitism, of perfection, around here,” he said. “People think that just by being here they’re automatically a little bit better than anyone else. But they’re not.” Rose’s resulting thesis was simple but devastating: the military’s festering morality crisis — evidenced by “pandemic drug addiction, racial tension, sedition, common crime, refusal of combat duty, widespread assaults and murders of officers [and] rapidly increasing desertion and decreasing reenlistments” — could be traced back to the transactional notions of honor perpetrated at places like West Point. His argument was crafted from a powerful combination of legalistic analysis and hundreds of vivid interviews from sources sketching out scenes that often seemed plucked from a hard-boiled police drama. Rose documented tainted honor board investigations and corrupt cadet interrogators, some of whom turned off their tape recorders to scream threats at defendants, forcibly cut their hair, and deprive them of sleep. One cadet said the pressure became so bad that he vomited. Others compared the experience to the mock prisoner-of-war interrogation training that school officials had instituted a few months earlier. Honor-code-related punishments were often biased and freighted with personal baggage. The chairman of one honor board stated his hostility toward a cadet on trial. “This guy has been in trouble before,” he said. “And we don’t want that kind around.” Cadets, many of them under twenty-one, who sought to appeal their honor board decisions were often threatened with a more serious military court-martial, which, due to the military justice system’s punishing and capricious nature, could entail imprisonment at Fort Leavenworth. Prosecution could stem from any number of offenses. Hundreds of regulations dictating cadet life were itemized in a standard-issue manual known as the Blue Book. Infractions were often vague, making them easily exploitable. They included “general inattention,” “carelessness,” and exercising “poor judgment.” Cadets were technically considered in violation of the honor code for asking a fellow cadet how to spell a word for an essay assignment, or for telling a fib. One cadet who told a superior he had done twenty push-ups when, in fact, he had done eighteen had the book thrown at him. Another who lied about shaving was expelled. Admitting one’s failings could also end in expulsion. “The code,” one West Pointer griped, “weeds out some cadets who are honest enough to report themselves for honor violations.” Even cadets who reported others for wrongdoing were sometimes expelled for “tolerating” bad behavior, imparting what some administrators quietly worried was a warped lesson, namely that “those who said ‘no comment’ or lied fared better than those who told the truth.” One West Point professor argued that these “seemingly purposeless rules breed resentment,” which in turn curdles into a full-blown rejection of morality. The honor code was a stand-in for respectable behavior, and yet cadets found it nearly impossible to stay in the code’s good graces. It could be fairly reasoned from here that the code was simply too rigid and that rule-breaking was the only way to survive. “Cadets,” Rose’s report concluded, “learn by example that deceit and deception are ‘standard operating procedure’ when the image of West Point or the Army is at stake.” His assertion was backed up by scores of cadets and even in-house psychiatrists. “I hear leaders talking about integrity and spirit and intent,” confessed one cadet. “But I see few who live by their preaching.” MacArthur’s high-minded crusade a generation earlier had led to something far more brutal and duplicitous than the “Athens on the Hudson” he had prescribed. As one commentator argued in Time magazine, the new batch of senior military leaders tasked with teaching ethics had become infamous for “falsifying body counts, concealing the bombing of Cambodia, [and] covering up My Lai.” At this time, West Point offered a single ethics course, an elective that was only available senior year. By the Vietnam War’s end , few cadets held MacArthurian feelings about honor. Sixty percent of West Point cadets, for instance, asserted in a 1974 survey that “adherence to the spirit of the Honor Code is deteriorating.” This, according to an accompanying study, could be traced back to the military’s “sanctimonious” belief in honor, which obscured the true knottiness of ethics. This was a generational loss of military integrity, and yet because it largely played out in academic environments, it often took the form of seemingly insignificant cheating rings. A series of major cheating scandals broke out at the service academies during the Cold War: in 1951, in 1967, in 1972, and then, not long after the fall of Saigon , in 1976. Air Force Academy Dean Robert McDermott defensively blamed the 1967 scandal on civilian counterculture, testifying to congressional investigators that dozens of identified cheaters had hailed from a clique “symbolized by kooky music, long hair, and a few other things.” A subsequent report penned by a committee of retired brass and academics disagreed, blaming the behavior on an academic environment concerned with “the symbols of achievement, sometimes at the expense of reality.” This shift in military culture was impossibly swift, evident in the case of West Point cadet Joseph Zengerle, whose hopes were high when, as a first-year plebe, he marched at John F. Kennedy’s 1961 inauguration. He absorbed, in person, Kennedy’s rousing call to “ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country.” Months later, he was there in the mess hall for General MacArthur’s humanistic farewell address. And yet shortly before his graduation from West Point, Zengerle marched at Kennedy’s funeral. The event presaged a darker politics and the continuation of a poisonous war, things that the man in the casket had tried to curb. Soon after, Zengerle was sent to Vietnam to be Westmoreland’s aide-de-camp. Rose’s report, meanwhile, was ignored, and the Air Force’s judge advocate general declined to certify him as a military lawyer. By the summer of 1974, brass had coerced him to resign. The deep issues Rose spotlighted continued bubbling up to the surface, often in the form of schoolyard deceptions. In 1976, more than 150 West Point cadets were charged with cheating, this time within the academy’s most storied and prestigious department: electrical engineering. Some assessments later indicated that as many as six hundred cadets had cheated, but even the smaller statistic qualified the 1976 affair as the worst cheating scandal in military history. One of the many cadets forced to resign was Robert K. Koster, son of Samuel Koster, an Army officer who helped cover up My Lai and previously ran West Point. After the war, many in the Pentagon fell victim to ego, blinkeredness, and historical revisionism. There was no reckoning with the war’s failures. This avoidance was typified by the POW-MIA movement, which, according to historian Rick Perlstein, was used “to justify the carnage in Vietnam in a way that rendered the United States as its sole victim.” Vietnam, along with the civil rights movement, saw the inflammation of the “Lost Cause” myth around the Civil War, manifested when President Nixon attempted to erect a monument to the Confederacy on West Point’s grounds. Today the warped lessons of the “Lost Cause” and POW-MIA continue to be nurtured by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , who has himself introduced a new fiction for his generation, namely that DEI was the major cause for America’s losses in Iraq and Afghanistan. Like MacArthur, Hegseth has made his own rhetorical paeans to honor, writing in his 2024 book The War on Warriors that it was a cornerstone commandment of “America’s civil religion.” By his definition, honor is for those with high casualty counts and reactionary politics. He wrote that honor was under threat from leftist causes, among them: “Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI), Critical Race Theory (CRT), feminism, genderism, safetyism, climate worship, manufactured ‘violent extremism,’ straight-up weirdo shit, and a grab bag of social justice causes.” Still, in a few fleeting paragraphs, Hegseth offers a cogent analysis of the rot, eloquently fusing MacArthur’s worries about military honesty with Eisenhower’s warnings about military spending. “Once you pin a star on your shoulder, the political pressure mounts,” Hegseth wrote. “Go-along-to-get-along, and get promoted, is the smoothest path. Don’t rock the boat, do what your political masters tell you, never admit mistakes — and get promoted. Then, once you retire, you get to collect a pension and a sweet job from Lockheed Martin.” In these pages, Hegseth proclaims that American generals should be statutorily restricted from comfortably migrating from their “comfy desk jobs in the Pentagon to the boardroom of the military-industrial complex.” It was a veiled swipe, perhaps, at President Joe Biden’s defense secretary, Lloyd Austin, who left a seat on Raytheon’s board to become the first black American to hold the position. A few months after his book was published, in November 2024, Hegseth was himself unexpectedly nominated to run the Pentagon. During his confirmation hearings, he sketched out how he would construct a hard-charging, unrepentantly violent, and blatantly ahistorical Department of War — departments of mere “defense” were no longer up to the task. In a flash, he dropped any of his past diagnoses about the Pentagon’s true problems, instead hypercharging all the agency’s worst qualities. Hegseth pushed the Pentagon budget past $1 trillion, retaliated against brass simply for their gender or skin color, engaged in war crimes, and prioritized his own future and personal vanity above all else, installing a makeup studio at the Pentagon and having government employees film his workouts and upload them to social media. Hegseth also barred from the Pentagon briefing room photographers who took unflattering photos of him. At one point during his confirmation hearing, US Senator Elizabeth Warren pressed Hegseth on his shifting stance regarding the dangers of military-industrial influence. “You’re quite sure that every general who serves should not go directly into the defense industry for ten years, but you’re not willing to make that same pledge?” she pressed. Hegseth smirked. “I’m not a general, Senator,” he said. One of the first things Hegseth did once in office was to crack down on academic freedom at places like West Point, banning books, pushing out professors, and reinterpreting the honor code. In a strange twist, a major ally in his fight is Michael Rose, who, under Biden, became a fierce critic of DEI policies and COVID-19 mandates. In little more than a year, Hegseth has done much damage, though the culture of the US Armed Forces was deeply compromised decades ago. For years, a certain subset of cadets has come to see deception as an ingrained part of military life, represented by a circulating joke about West Point’s motto that goes “Duty, Country, Hon — well, two out of three ain’t bad.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Against the Politics of Communal Fear
articles.author: Bhaskar Sunkara
articles.content: New York City’s new municipal strategy to combat antisemitism comes just days after the war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu used his platform at the United Nations to call Zohran Mamdani “the antisemitic mayor of New York” and claim that since his election “many Jews no longer feel safe” in the city. The initiative seeks to expand education, support victims of hate crimes, and fund security at Jewish institutions and other houses of worship throughout the five boroughs. Laudable as any attempt to reduce animus is, the Left should view the plan skeptically. Antisemitism, it goes without saying, is an evil. And it’s an evil that socialists have particular reason to be concerned with. For centuries, the idea that powerful Jewish interests were at the heart of social injustice was widespread. Socialists of August Bebel’s generation called antisemitism “the socialism of fools” for how it steered resentment of capitalist instability and speculation into ethnic hatred. Today Mamdani is right to condemn it. And it is understandable that he wants to give that condemnation a practical policy expression. This makes sense on the level of both principle and tactics for a political leader who has been the subject of a deliberate and baseless attempt to equate his support for Palestinian freedom with antisemitism. Any socialist mayor should oppose prejudice, enforce equal rights, and respond to specific acts of discrimination or violence. The question is whether the administration’s response is proportionate to the problem, and whether its rhetoric helps people assess their circumstances accurately or encourages them to understand their lives through a sense of communal siege. Assessing the Threat The strategy, produced by the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism, coordinates work across schools, the police, civil rights authorities, and other agencies through an interagency task force. It doubles funding for the broader Partners Against the Hate grants program to $6.4 million and allocates $1 million for security at nonprofits, including synagogues and other houses of worship. Notably, the report explicitly defends New Yorkers’ right to protest and doesn’t adopt the flawed International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, which has been used to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism. Its commitment to enforcing civil rights and teaching Jewish American history also deserves support. But its account of Jewish insecurity and its outsourcing of much of its work through third-sector organization deserves scrutiny. Since October 7, 2023, political discourse in New York has been disproportionately concerned with the supposed threats to Jewish New Yorkers, particularly from supporters of Palestinian liberation and Muslim New Yorkers. The campaign against Mamdani intensified that tendency. A secular socialist was portrayed as a Jew-hating Islamist because of his Muslim background and support for Palestinian self-determination. The Israeli government and its supporters, who identify the Jewish people with a violent state, have deliberately blurred the line between being challenged for controversial views (say, defending a genocidal state on a college campus) and being hounded for one’s religious identity. In reality, NORC research found that people on the hard right held significantly more antisemitic attitudes than other Americans, while those on the hard left held more anti-Israel views. Still, it’s reasonable to say that amid rising authoritarianism, a right-wing administration, and anger at Israel’s actions, certain forms of antisemitism have grown. These range from naked bigotry to the subtler reification of identity involved in asking Jewish New Yorkers born in the American republic, six thousand miles away, to repent for Israel’s murderous actions. A real social problem, however, can also acquire the dimensions of a moral panic, and that panic can be weaponized against the Left. Consider a recent example: like other Americans, Asian Americans were victims of violence, some of it racially motivated. Yet the rise of the “Stop Asian Hate” movement brought sweeping claims about what it meant to be Asian in America, rooted in collective vulnerability and identitarian remedies. Reported hate crimes against Asians did rise during the pandemic amid Donald Trump’s anti-China rhetoric. But the mobilization against those real acts also encouraged a salience bias, in which seemingly every street altercation involving an Asian victim was viewed as a targeted hate crime. Yet one widely cited tally, from Stop AAPI Hate, consisted mostly of verbal harassment ; physical assaults made up about 16 percent of the nearly eleven thousand incidents reported to the organization from March 2020 through December 2021. Hate crimes against Asians recorded by the NYPD rose sharply , from twenty-eight in 2020 to well over a hundred in 2021. But the movement went further, presenting those attacks as a wave of racist hostility directed at a single community. “Asian American and Pacific Islander” is an umbrella label that groups together people with origins across a vast region, divided by class, language, and national background. The “Stop Asian Hate” remedies were tautological. The movement insisted there was a mass problem that demanded marches and won corporate declarations against hate, new federal hate crime legislation, and pork for community nonprofits. It didn’t matter that some of the most high-profile incidents fit the story poorly. In January 2022, Michelle Go was murdered while waiting for a train at Times Square. The man charged with pushing her in front of the train was homeless and had been diagnosed with schizophrenia two decades earlier. A better-staffed public transit system, track barriers, more state funding for psychiatric care, and supportive housing might all have helped prevent Go’s murder. Public education about the contributions of an imagined “AAPI community” would not have. But organizing around identity made those universal solutions harder, not easier, to imagine. And it taught many Asian Americans to feel irrationally unsafe in the cities and towns where they grew up and to understand their safety in racial terms. The same dynamics are at play in discussions of antisemitism today. When something happens to a Jewish New Yorker, the first response is seemingly to present the incident as evidence of an all-encompassing danger, making other Jews feel less secure. That fear itself then becomes politically noteworthy: “I don’t feel safe in the city of my birth anymore.” Communal identity becomes even more central to how people understand their lives and their relationships with others. The statistics often cited in response to arguments like these also deserve scrutiny. Advocacy groups’ incident tallies, police records of hate crimes, and surveys of communal anxiety measure different things. Yet in a climate of fear — whether among Asian Americans a few years ago or Jewish people today — they are conflated into evidence of an emergency. The Anti-Defamation League’s 2021 audit is instructive. It highlighted a worrying 34 percent increase in antisemitic incidents while acknowledging that many of the incidents were identified through new reporting partnerships . Putting aside well-warranted left-wing skepticism of the ADL, the example shows how changes in data collection can complicate efforts to distinguish changes in underlying behavior from changes in reporting. Even police data on hate crimes don’t necessarily tell us how likely an Asian American or Jewish New Yorker is to suffer violence. That requires attention to absolute numbers, population, the kinds of offenses involved, and their distribution. It also requires political judgments about whether the response should take the form of universal or identitarian investments, and how those investments should be delivered. The report’s own rhetoric illustrates some of the confusion. Its opening letters move between assaults, vandalism, and “stares and casual comments” in describing a climate of fear. These experiences require different assessments and responses. Surveys showing widespread anxiety cannot independently establish the prevalence of the conditions people fear. Otherwise, the effects of alarm become its justification. It doesn’t require ignoring the persistence of antisemitism and the potential for its mass emergence to say that American Jews live in secure, prosperous, and integrated settings. Some heinous speech and sporadic violence should not erase the distance between today’s America and the history of Jewish exclusion. As Hannah Arendt warned, treating antisemitism as an eternal fact of Jewish life can give antisemites an alibi, making a contingent political prejudice appear natural and inevitable. Ahistorical comparisons trivialize the centuries of subordination, pogroms, and ultimately mass extermination that Jews faced in Europe. Along with anti-American rhetoric like Joe Biden’s absurd claim that without Israel “not a Jew in the world is safe,” such comparisons do a disservice to the long struggle that has made the United States a hospitable home for millions of minorities. The panics that made some Asians afraid of commuting to work, or some Jewish New Yorkers afraid of their neighbors, also rely on rhetoric that leaves us little room to describe a resurgence of structural discrimination. If there is a real antisemitic political movement growing in this country, beyond the acts of a few depraved people, what anti-Jewish laws is it advancing? How is it organizing to deprive Jews of their rights? What social structures are being built to enforce Jewish exclusion? Online bigotry from people like Nick Fuentes, or even from some supporters of the Palestinian cause, does not itself demonstrate a mass movement capable of imposing anti-Jewish rule. Nor does it establish how much that bigotry affects Jewish Americans’ daily lives beyond the cycle of panic and the reification of identity it encourages. Cherry-picking speech in a country of more than 340 million people, even when every report is accurate, obscures the broader state of our society. The Universalist Answer There is always a danger of accepting our opponents’ misleading accounts of a city rife with hate and communal strife. But Mamdani’s response — that he is the mayor for all New Yorkers — makes both moral and tactical sense. The city’s policy choices, however, deserve scrutiny. The Left’s answer to communal fear should be a radical assertion of our shared humanity, the same assertion we employ to defend the rights of the starved and maimed people of Palestine. When we encourage an environment where every political discussion has to start with “as a Jew” or “as a Muslim,” we’ve already accepted the idea that our moral obligations have communal boundaries. Among Jewish critics of Israel, the habit is understandable: they are answering a state that falsely claims to speak for Jews everywhere. But no one should have to establish the right ancestry or religion before opposing the killing of Palestinians, just as no one needs to be Jewish to be outraged by a swastika on a synagogue door. The growth of identitarian rhetoric challenges our broader effort to change New York, a city long shaped by ethnic brokerage through organizations that claim to speak for particular communities. Today that pattern rewards those who can demonstrate not only their group’s political power but also its vulnerability. The spokespeople are, of course, often professionals and capitalists speaking to workers. When city and state governments accept this arrangement, they’re boosting a form of multiculturalism that amounts to: “Hello, Bengali worker, would you feel more comfortable if the city spoke to you via your Bengali slumlord?” Every new program premised on a communal threat invites other groups’ brokers to make the same case. Socialists should be trying to wind down this system and build organizations on the basis of class identity, not reinforce it in the name of diversity. This is where Mamdani has been a breath of fresh air. The media constantly talked about his identity and made him address it. But he is most comfortable translating his core universalism into concrete class demands: cheaper rents, free public transit, and universal childcare. In its delivery mechanisms, however, this new plan to address antisemitism is a (very small) step in the wrong direction. It channels millions through nonprofit organizations for work public agencies could do directly. Some of these organizations are particularly pernicious, like the Jewish Community Relations Council of New York, which explicitly works to build support for Israel and circulates material opposing boycott campaigns against it. No one on the Left should support sending taxpayer funds to such an organization. But even if all the groups were committed solely to hate crime prevention and survivor support, we should ask why public agencies aren’t equipped to meet those needs directly. This gets to a wider problem. New York responds to social needs by funneling money through nonprofits, often leaving public agencies to administer contracts instead of developing the ability to provide services themselves. Its own investigators have documented conflicts of interest and oversight failures in the nonprofit shelter system. Those failures strengthen the case for a better-funded welfare state that delivers services directly. A socialist administration should build durable public capacity to address real social problems without reifying either communal identity or the perception of insecurity. In this case, civil rights enforcement and public education campaigns should be carried out entirely by staffed public institutions with transparent budgets and clear performance indicators. Whatever our assessment of the prevalence of antisemitism in our city, Jewish New Yorkers are entitled to the same freedoms as everyone else, and violations of those freedoms should be addressed. We can uphold those commitments without fueling communalism, by building institutions that improve people’s lives and give them the choice to relate to their identity, or choose not to, in any way that they want. articles.title: A Decade After His First Presidential Run, Bernie Isn’t Alone
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: If you’re anyone who veers remotely to the left politically, there are two eras: a time before Bernie Sanders ran for president, and a time after. The US political landscape before Sanders’s first presidential campaign looks today like an alien planet. There were virtually no socialists who held elected office, or at least those who admitted to it. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) was an obscure organization with a little over six thousand members across twenty-six chapters. Arguably the most prominent leftist figure was a curmudgeonly linguist who almost never appeared in mainstream media, Noam Chomsky. Only 59 percent of Democrats and less than half of independents were willing to vote for a socialist candidate. And the great progressive hope was a politician who flatly opposed single-payer health care and ran on a platform of stronger regulation and more public investment in key industries. Within five years of Sanders’s run, dozens of open socialists served in elected office at every level of government, including the US Congress. DSA’s membership had exploded to more than 55,000 with more than 150 chapters in every corner of the country. Socialists like Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were among the most popular political figures in the country. The share of Democrats willing to vote for a socialist candidate had jumped to 74 percent . And that progressive politician, Elizabeth Warren, launched a presidential campaign on a platform of single-payer health care, universal childcare, free public college, and debt cancellation. Neither Sanders nor his campaign were single-handedly responsible for all this. But it’s not a coincidence that the political landscape transformed this drastically, in this particular way, within less than a decade of his first campaign, nor that 97 percent of DSA’s now 120,000-strong membership joined after 2016 (the majority of its current members joined after 2019, when Sanders launched his second run and a year after Ocasio-Cortez first won election). Before Sanders made his first official announcement — to a small crowd of Capitol Hill reporters, muttering that there wasn’t an “endless amount of time” because he’d have to get back to work — most people, even on the Left, would have told you the world we currently inhabit, with all its horrors but also its sudden possibility, was decades away at best. There were a few socialists in political office before Sanders ran. Kshama Sawant had won a seat on the Seattle city council in 2013, for instance, while Carlos Ramirez-Rosa was sworn into his Chicago alderman’s seat twenty-nine days before Sanders’s announcement, even if he had not run as a socialist. (Ramirez-Rosa joined DSA a few months after Donald Trump won the 2016 election.) But the broad national appeal of Sanders’s platform was something different. It reminded millions of Americans who had learned to instinctively narrow their political ambitions that the things they assumed were impossible — not because they were actually impractical, but because there seemingly wasn’t the political will — they could and should fight for, because it was what most people wanted. Sanders’s campaign showed it was possible for a socialist to win over people who had never even flirted with New Deal liberalism, let alone Marxism. Whatever drove it, whether Sanders’ authenticity, his fist-shaking against the establishment, or the fact that even conservative households don’t want to be buried alive in medical bills, Sanders had a crossover appeal that defied the way we tend to pigeonhole voters. It wasn’t out of the ordinary to hear Trump supporters in those years professing that, after the demagogic billionaire, Bernie was their guy. Ideas and policies were one thing, but Sanders gave today’s socialists a ready-made vocabulary and approach to sell them, too. The Left’s decades in the political wilderness had been an often fruitless, Goldilocks-style search for a political tribune. Before Sanders, the lefty firebrands who championed the causes he became famous for came off, however unfairly , as kooks — like Dennis Kucinich, whose penchant for ventriloquism and claims he had seen a UFO could overshadow his advocacy for single-payer health care, or Mike Gravel, whose antiwar message was undercut by an onstage style that came off as unhinged ranting. Lefty politicians either had vision but not credibility, or, in Warren’s case, credibility but without a sufficiently ambitious vision. Sanders, by contrast, came off as fairly normal but serious — neither an ideological zealot, nor a doctrinaire leftist who spoke in slogans or obscure jargon, but someone who put socialist ideas into everyday language and made you agree they were common sense. What eccentricities he had built up in the course of a lifetime were either helpful — the uncombed hair, rumpled suits, and distaste for chit-chat that so amused political reporters bolstered his image as a no-nonsense fighter — or ones he swiftly repudiated . As Americans watched and heard Sanders speak with their own eyes and ears, they didn’t see the caricature of a socialist they had been fed through popular culture, but a pissed-off fighter for the working Americans being perennially screwed by a host of nefarious forces they recognized in their own lives: big banks, health insurers, corrupt politicians, the billionaires that fund them. This had been the secret sauce of Sanders’s breakthrough election to the US Congress in 1990, when he had used the previous year’s savings and loan bailout as a political foil and saw passing motorists yell at him to “Give ’em hell, Bernie!” They also saw someone who rooted this pitch in a national tradition they understood. Yes, Sanders often pointed to European countries like Denmark and Sweden to show that the policies he was calling for were practical. But crucially, he wrapped himself in the coat of the New Deal, the most well-known historical parallel to what he envisioned for the country, eschewing the tendency of some radicals to dismiss Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s program as a series of mere liberal reforms that had done capitalism a favor. In his first run, just as he would in his second, Sanders delivered a major address explaining to the nation what democratic socialism meant by casting the national memory back to the New Deal. Sanders had good reason to do it beyond its historical legibility for American voters. After all, for all its compromises, the greatest, longest-lasting achievements of Roosevelt’s program were often demanded , drawn up , and put into motion by left-wing radicals. It took a little longer for the class of young socialists inspired by Sanders to absorb all of these lessons. Many clung to the judgmental moralism and jargon-littered vocabulary that became accepted as normal on the Left for far too long. And socialists’ self-defeating fixation on “abolition” of police and prisons still persists, in spite of its many political and practical downsides . But they have been absorbed. We see it in the more plainspoken communication style and more class-focused approach of Ocasio-Cortez, who these days tends to stress the power of billionaires instead of simply racism to explain the Right’s ascent, and who is more likely to talk about how “the American Revolution was against the billionaires of their time” than to talk about “the intersectionality of interconnectedness of all our fights” for a laundry list of types of justice. And we see it in the mayoralty of Zohran Mamdani, one the most popular politicians in the country, who has charted a different path on public safety and policing that more closely parallels that of Sanders, whose very first election victory rested on poaching the local police union’s endorsement. Keeping the Light Alive All of the elements that built and sustained Sanders’s political path through an era vastly more unfriendly to socialism were there in his first campaign. That campaign in turn became a real-world model for socialists in the twenty-first century to both run for office and engage with a skeptical American public — a model that, looking out from the cliffside of 2026, they have used to reshape US politics. Trump’s two election victories and the weakness of liberal institutions have made it easy to miss this story. It’s been made even easier thanks to a mainstream press perpetually in a hurry to declare the Left dead, confidently telling us over and over again that the socialist movement Sanders’s run helped breathe new life into had finally run out of oxygen. The reality is that a decade after a time when, generously, only a handful of socialists around the country held any elected office, socialists now hold serious positions of power all over. There will be at least seven socialists in the US House of Representatives next year, growing nearly fourfold since Trump declared to a standing ovation from Congress that “America will never be a socialist country.” A socialist will almost certainly be elected mayor of the nation’s capital this November. Socialists are presidents of the city councils of both St Louis, Missouri, and Providence, Rhode Island, with the candidate’s slate of progressive allies achieving a near sweep of their city council races in the latter. Socialists also control a third of Portland, Oregon’s city council, occupy nearly a third of the seats on Minneapolis’s — where DSA-backed members serve as both the majority and minority leaders — and have four seats on Los Angeles’s fifteen-member city council. Wisconsin has a socialist caucus again in its state legislature after a nearly hundred-year absence, one of whose members very nearly took the Democratic nomination for governor this year. For years, socialists held a near-majority on the city council of Somerville, Massachusetts. Numbering in the dozens at the end of last decade, there are now more than 250 socialists holding elected office across the country. You can find them everywhere from the Mountain States (in Santa Fe , Missoula , Aurora , to name a few) and the Midwest (in Toledo , Louisville , Iowa , Chicago , among others) to New England (in places like Portland , Cambridge , the state legislatures of Vermont and Connecticut ), and the South (in New Orleans , Atlanta , Knoxville , San Antonio , and more). And of course, in New York, a socialist governs the country’s biggest city, the home of its financial sector and the largest city economy in the world, helped by four fellow socialists on its city council and a total of sixteen who will sit in the state legislature after November. Long before this, with much smaller numbers, socialists in the state, including Mamdani himself, had already played leading roles in major progressive legislative victories, passing sweeping eviction protections and allowing the state’s largest public utility to enter the renewable energy industry, among other things. Many of these officials were directly inspired by Sanders. Ocasio-Cortez, Rep. Summer Lee, former fellow Squad member Cori Bush, and Massachusetts state representative Erika Uyterhoeven all volunteered or worked on his 2016 run. Mamdani has pointed squarely at that campaign as the reason he became a socialist. Other socialist mayors-to-be, like Providence’s David Morales and Washington, DC’s Janeese Lewis George , have credited it with their political awakening. So have socialist Squad-member-in-waiting Claire Valdez and St Petersburg city council member Richie Floyd , the first socialist elected in Florida in a hundred years. Go to any moderately large gathering of socialists, whether elected officials, rank-and-file DSAers, or both, and you’re likely to see “Bernie 2016” memorabilia sprinkled throughout. Attached again to concrete policies and living, flesh-and-blood political figures, socialism is not the boogeyman it used to be. Most Democratic voters, a third of whom now identify as democratic socialists, are perfectly happy to have a socialist as their candidate, or even actively prefer a candidate endorsed by one. Multiple polls show voters across the board are more turned off by MAGA candidates and Trump endorsees than self-described democratic socialists. In both pure numbers and political power, the current crop of socialist elected officials may be far away from the movement’s American zenith in the early twentieth century, but none of this suggests they’re anywhere close to hitting their ceiling yet. Onward and Upward? The question is whether they and the movement around them can sustain this upward trajectory. In some ways, Sanders’s path to the presidential race, spread out over thirty-five years in which socialists wandered the desert, was easier than the one his political heirs now have to traverse. Not only is state repression of the Left ramping up to levels far beyond where it was even under Ronald Reagan, but high-profile socialists are today as likely to face attacks and misinformation coming from pockets of the Left as from the Right. Sanders too spent his career being pelted by many of the same left-wing accusations his 2020s successors now face: that he was a traitor to the cause, an imperialist, a liberal, a fraud, too accommodationist to the Democratic Party, and so on. Lobbed at a time when the Left was small and marginal, none of it stuck by the time Sanders ran in 2015, when he was viewed in the fresh eyes of both friend and foe as a uniquely, even naively, principled and pure idealist — instead of the shrewd, ruthlessly pragmatic operator he actually was. It was just as well. An unyielding pragmatic radicalism has always been at the heart of Sanders’s approach. As he followed its glow, millions of others trailed after its familiar incandescence. And when the light grew just bright enough, he turned around and saw something remarkable: that he was no longer alone. articles.title: Jordan Bardella Isn’t Such a Friend of Jews After All
articles.author: Marlon Ettinger
articles.content: As a young member of the Front National (today’s Rassemblement National), Jordan Bardella was an “obsessive antisemite,” according to a story published by investigative site Mediapart this Monday. “Banks are all controlled by Jews,” Bardella allegedly wrote in one message published by Mediapart . “The Jew must dominate other peoples, crush them and rob them,” read another. “A Zionist is necessarily Jewish, and deeply so.” Bardella, who was the Rassemblement National’s candidate for prime minister in 2024 and who has been president of the party since 2022, denies having written the messages, which Mediapart says date from between 2013 and 2015. “These comments are completely outrageous. They’re not mine. . . . I dispute them,” Bardella said in a television interview on Monday night , adding that his lawyers had filed a defamation lawsuit against Mediapart . “I think we’re looking at something very organized . . . which resembles a covert operation.” Bardella also claimed that the messages that he says he didn’t write, when he was around seventeen years old, weren’t from a time when he had any sort of leadership position in the party. Bardella joined Jean-Marie Le Pen’s Front National when he was sixteen, then became head of the Seine-Saint-Denis branch of the party in 2014, when he was nineteen. During his rise as the fresh young face of the far-right party, Bardella was feted in the media as a representative of a new version of the Front National that had shed its roots in the fascist underworld to become a party like any other, free from its racist heritage. “They present a young, cosmopolitan . . . image for the Front National,” the news channel BFMTV wrote in 2016 about a group of party activists from France’s suburbs. “Their figurehead: Jordan Bardella, regional councilor for Île-de-France [the region around Paris] at just twenty-one.” At about the same time, according to Mediapart , Bardella was swimming in a soup of late 2000s and early 2010s French “new right” ideology, which has close affiliations with fascism and classic French antisemitism. Its chief ideologue, Alain Soral, became a viral celebrity online for his syncretic analysis of French society, which wed racist, anti-immigrant ideology to a type of motley anti-Zionism based fundamentally in antisemitism, with a few anti-imperialist geopolitical positions soldered on. In the late 2000s, Soral was close with and wrote speeches for Jean-Marie Le Pen, still the party’s leader then. Soral became a member of the Front National’s central committee but left in 2009 when he was denied leadership of the party’s list for the European elections. “His analyses are correct because everything is verified by the facts,” Bardella wrote of Soral in 2013, per Mediapart . “Zionism and domination by the banks are linked (Goldman Sachs, Rothschild, Lehman Brothers. . . . ).” “I knew Bardella a little; I had some conversations with him,” Soral said in 2025 . “On certain radical subjects, he wasn’t as innocent as he seems.” “Jordan watched kilometers of Soral videos and read his books,” a former “close adviser” to Bardella told Mediapart . “He became politicized partially because of it.” Le Pen’s Biggest Regret Marine Le Pen, the party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, expelled her father from the Front National in 2015 after he refused to apologize for calling the gas chambers in the Holocaust a “detail” of history that didn’t matter much then defended Marshal Philippe Pétain, the general who collaborated with the Nazis during the World War II–era occupation of France. Jean-Marie Le Pen’s expulsion was supposed to represent the culmination of this strategy of “ dédiabolisation” — literally “de-demonization.” The National Rally may have been founded by at least one former member of the Waffen-SS, the message was, but Le Pen père ’s expulsion was the end result of a cleanup operation by Le Pen fille to push out the embarrassing remnants who were still partial to a Roman salute every once in a while (“I’ll never forgive my decision [to expel my father], because I know that it caused him an immense amount of pain,” Le Pen said in 2025). In the 2010s, Louis Aliot theorized that shedding the Front National’s antisemitic image was one of the last barriers it had to surmount to become electable. Aliot visited Israel — a first for a politician from his party — and actively cultivated links with Israel’s political class. Aliot, who once lived with Marine Le Pen and still has an excellent relationship with her family, is today vice president of the Rassemblement National as well as mayor of Perpignan. He continues to play an influential role in the party, which has wholeheartedly adopted the strategy of pushing Zionism as a defense against historical charges of antisemitism. Marine Le Pen has called the party the “shield” of Jews in France against radical Islam, painting France’s Arab and Muslim population as a threat to Jews, an echo of familiar neoconservative narratives of a “clash of civilizations.” As president of the party, Bardella has kept the ship steady and continued to present the Rassemblement National as French Jews’ best ally, mostly through ostentatious pro-Zionist posturing. In 2025, Bardella visited Jerusalem as an official representative for the party at an Israeli government-sponsored conference on fighting antisemitism. That’s the angle that the party, which fallen into formation to claim Mediapart ’s story is a hoax, is taking to defend Bardella. “I saw him at Yad Vashem, at the Nova site, in the kibbutz of Netiv HaAsara slain on October 7 . . . then in Jerusalem to bring the voice of our party into the fight against antisemitism,” a parliamentary assistant for the Rassemblement National in the EU Parliament posted . “The controversies will pass. What I saw and heard there nobody can take away.” “ Mediapart is a far-left newspaper,” the party’s vice president, Aliot, told me on Tuesday, after I asked if the Rassemblement National believed the accusations against Bardella were true. “No comment.” Mediapart responded by saying that if its credibility continued to be questioned, it would be releasing the documents that it based its reporting on. Erik Tegnér, the founder of a far-right media organization called Frontières , posted that Bardella was essentially the target of right-wing elected officials who regularly leaked to Mediapart , amid speculation that the story could have been planted by Le Pen and her allies to push Bardella out of the party after tensions following her decision to run for president. Has the Rassemblement National Changed? Meanwhile, it’s egg on the face for France’s liberals and centrists who’ve made a big show about the party’s evolution into becoming a responsible party of government. Serge Klarsfeld, a French historian and lawyer who spent his career chasing Nazi war criminals and documenting France’s role in deporting Jews during the Holocaust, drew condemnation from many when he met with Marine Le Pen in 2024, then said he would vote “without hesitation” for the Rassemblement National over the left-wing France Insoumise. “The RN supports Jews, supports the state of Israel. It’s normal that between an antisemitic party and a pro-Jewish party, I’d vote for the pro-Jewish party,” Klarsfeld said. False critiques of Jean-Luc Mélenchon and France Insoumise have multiplied since October 2023 because of the party’s support for Palestine and condemnation of Israel’s genocide. A frequent accusation against France Insoumise these days is that it, and not the Rassemblement National, is today the party of antisemitism in France. This attitude is said to be fueled by a desire for votes from young Arab, African, and Muslim voters in the poor suburbs who are susceptible to a Soralite blend of anti-Zionism. That’s despite France Insoumise’s clear rejection of antisemitism and the doubtful prospect that this caricatured electorate actually exists. Meanwhile, the Rassemblement National coasts on a reputation promoted endlessly by figures in the media and the government that it has changed and is no longer a racist or antisemitic force. “The Rassemblement National belongs to the republican arc,” Bruno Retailleau — who was Emmanuel Macron’s interior minister across multiple governments, and is president of the mainstream conservative party Les Républicains — said last summer, using a phrase that means a party is within the realm of legitimate political expression in France. Retailleau, a particularly noxious anti-immigrant French nationalist, may offer better proof that France’s conservatives have radicalized than that anything fundamental has changed about the Rassemblement National. “Politics is communication,” Bardella reportedly wrote in the messages over a decade ago. “Ever since [Marine Le Pen’s] speech got cleaned up the number of voters has exploded,” he explained, while celebrating that the party “has stayed true to its founding ideology” for “more than 40 years.” He might insist otherwise today, but I think he was on to something.
